<explanation>
Based on the provided project details, here’s how to create an accurate system design/architecture diagram tailored for this AI-empowered stock analysis tool built with Wails and NaiveUI:

1. Identify the Project Type and Purpose:
   • The project is a full-stack desktop application built with a Go backend using Wails to integrate with a modern web-based frontend. The purpose is to provide AI-powered stock analysis for markets such as A-shares, Hong Kong stocks, and US stocks, integrating multiple APIs (e.g., for stock data, AI models, news crawling, etc.) while providing interactive user experiences via NaiveUI / Vue.
   • The README stresses integration with various AI models (OpenAI, Ollama, LMStudio, etc.) and emphasizes stock market data and multi-platform support.

2. Analyze the File Structure:
   • Top-Level Indicators:
     – The project has a clear separation between frontend and backend directories.
     – Several build scripts and platform-specific files (e.g., app_darwin.go, app_linux.go, Windows installer scripts) indicate cross-platform build support.
     – Presence of a “wails.json” suggests project configuration for the Wails framework.
   • Backend Directory:
     – Contains multiple subdirectories such as “data” (for different API integrations like alert, crawler, dingding, stock data, etc.), “db” (for database connectivity or persistence), “logger” (for logging functionality), and “models” (defining the data structures).
     – The API implementations (e.g., fund_data_api, tushare_data_api) are distinct and each comes with its own test files.
   • Frontend Directory:
     – Contains Vue components (App.vue, components like about.vue, fund.vue, settings.vue, stock.vue) and a router configuration which is built using Vite.
     – The “wailsjs” folder shows that Wails generates JavaScript and TypeScript bindings for Go code, bridging the frontend with backend methods.
   • Shared and Infrastructure Elements:
     – The main Go files at the root (app.go, main.go) serve as entry points.
     – Build and scripts directories contain platform-specific deployment/build scripts.

3. Key Architectural Components to Include:
   • Frontend Layer:
     - Vue.js-based user interface built with NaiveUI, with configuration via Vite.
     - Routing and components (for displaying stock data, AI analysis results, settings, etc.).
     - Interfaces (wailsjs) to invoke Go backend functions.
   • Backend Layer:
     - Go business logic implemented via multiple packages:
       ▪ Data Layer: Different API clients (OpenAI, crawler, Tushare, etc.) for fetching or processing stock and financial data.
       ▪ Models: Data structures and domain models.
       ▪ Logger: Logging subsystem.
       ▪ Database: Data persistence or storage abstraction.
     - Platform-specific variations (files like app_darwin.go and app_linux.go) to handle OS-specific functionality.
   • Integration & Communication:
     - Communication between the frontend and backend through the Wails runtime.
     - APIs wrapping external services like OpenAI, Dingding, etc.
   • CI/CD and Build Processes:
     - GitHub workflows (in .github/workflows) for continuous integration.
     - Scripts for building on various platforms (macOS arm/intel, Windows, etc.).

4. Creating the System Design Diagram:
   a. Main Components:
     - Label “Frontend” to include all Vue/NaiveUI components, router, and wailsjs integration. Emphasize that this is the user interaction layer.
     - Label “Backend” to include Go components, grouped by sub-packages: Data (various API integrations), Models, Logger, Database, and Platform-Specific Adapters.
     - Draw “External Services” as a separate box listing APIs and data sources (OpenAI, Tushare, Dingding, etc.).
     - Optionally add “CI/CD Pipeline” to denote GitHub workflows and build scripts.
   
   b. Relationships and Data Flow:
     - Draw directional arrows from the Frontend to the Backend to represent API calls via the Wails runtime. Label these arrows as “Wails bindings” or “RPC”.
     - From the Backend, draw arrows to “External Services” denoting API calls (such as AI model requests, stock data retrieval, and news crawling).
     - Represent internal interactions within the backend – for example, the Data layer interacting with Models and Logger – using arrows or connecting lines.
   
   c. Architectural Patterns & Design Principles:
     - Highlight the separation of concerns (frontend vs. backend).
     - The modular design in the backend: separate directories for data access, logging, and models, which suggests an organized architecture similar to MVC or layered architecture.
     - The usage of platform-specific entry points for customized builds is also a notable design choice.
   
   d. Relevant Technologies:
     - Frontend: Vue, NaiveUI, Vite.
     - Backend: Go, Wails framework, and various third-party APIs (OpenAI, Tushare, etc.).
     - Build & CI: GitHub Actions, shell scripts for cross-platform builds, and configuration through wails.json.
   
5. Guidelines for Tailoring the Diagram:
   - For this full-stack application, clearly separate the frontend (user interaction, view, and route management) from the backend (business logic, API integrations, and data management).
   - Emphasize how the Wails framework bridges the Go backend to the Vue-based frontend. Consider drawing a “bridge” component between the two.
   - Keep the diagram detailed by identifying as many internal components as possible; for example, within the backend, show separate modules for “API Clients”, “Database Interface”, “Logging”, and “Model Definitions.”
   - Identify colored shapes (e.g., rectangles for components, cylinders for databases, arrows for calls) to improve clarity.
   
6. Elements to Include in the Final Diagram:
   - Use clear, descriptive labels for each component (e.g., "Frontend (Vue + NaiveUI)", "Backend Data API (Stock/Tushare/OpenAI)", "Logger", "Database", "Wails Runtime Bridge").
   - Include directional arrows to show the flow from the user interface to the backend and out to external services.
   - Optionally use color coding or different shapes to distinguish between the frontend, backend services, external APIs, and build/infrastructure components.
   
By following these detailed instructions, you can create a comprehensive and visually clear system design diagram that covers all essential architectural elements of the go-stock application. Make sure to balance clarity and detail by avoiding too much abstraction—include as many key components as possible while ensuring the diagram remains readable and functional for maintenance and further architectural discussions.
</explanation>
